hook.line: Pachisi, India's cross-shaped race game, takes its name from its biggest throw, 25 — and it is the ancestor of Ludo all over the world.
hook.say: Let me show you the game of the Indian courts!

ch.say: An emperor used his courtyard as the board!
p: Pachisi is an old Indian race game on a cross-shaped board, a cousin of chaupar, which uses long dice; in pachisi you throw cowrie shells.

The Mughal emperor Akbar (16th century) is said to have played on a giant courtyard board at Fatehpur Sikri with costumed people as pieces. In the 19th century the game reached Britain and spread worldwide as Ludo.

ch.say: Roll a 6 to bring a piece out!
ch.cap: A Ludo board: a yard in each corner; round the track clockwise, then up your own colour to the centre
p: Ludo is for 2–4 players. A 6 brings a piece out; then move by the roll. Land on a rival to send it home; star squares are safe.
Pachisi is played on a cloth cross (each arm 3 × 8 squares). Pieces start in the central charkoni, go once round and come back. Castles marked with a cross are safe.
